deep.reconstruction:
The page is a set of Euler-characteristic bookkeeping exercises for cell decompositions of surfaces, and for how those decompositions lift to double covers branched at vertices. It sits inside a 1983 sequence on Teichmüller theory and 'cartes'. The previous page sets up the correspondence between trivalent maps, triangulated maps and covers of P^1 branched over 0,1,∞, together with the reflection group <σ0,σ1,σ2> used for real (R-)curves.

(1) Top block: four-holed sphere. The picture shows two pairs of pants glued along a curve, i.e. a sphere with 4 holes. Each pants is cut into 2 hexagons, giving the stated decomposition: 4 hexagons, 16 edges, 10 vertices.
- Check: χ = 10 − 16 + 4 = −2, correct for a 4-holed sphere.
- Edge count: 24 hexagon sides = 2·(interior edges) + (boundary edges), with 16 edges in total. This gives 8 interior and 8 boundary edges.
- 4 of the vertices are marked 'ramifiés'. The double cover branched exactly there has 2·10 − 4 = 16 vertices, 32 edges and 8 hexagons.
- Check: χ = 16 − 32 + 8 = −8 = 2(−2) − 4, consistent with Riemann–Hurwitz.

(2) Pair of pants. A pair of pants is 2 hexagons, 9 edges, 6 vertices, so χ = −1. From 12 sides = 2i + b with i + b = 9, there are 3 interior edges (the seams) and 6 boundary arcs. This is the classical decomposition of a pair of pants into two right-angled hexagons glued along alternate sides.

(3) Bottom right: sphere to torus. The sphere has 6 vertices, 8 edges and 4 faces. Grothendieck first wrote 'triangles' and corrected it to 'carrés' (squares). So χ = 2.
- Four vertices are branch points of degree 2; the other two have degree 4. Degree sum = 4·2 + 2·4 = 16 = 2·8, consistent.
- The double cover branched at the 4 degree-2 vertices has 8 vertices, all of order 4, plus 16 edges and 8 squares. So χ = 0: a torus carrying a regular {4,4} square map.
- This is the elliptic curve as a double cover of P^1 branched at 4 points (pillowcase picture), seen combinatorially.
- A first annotation 'dont 4 d'ordre 4' was struck out, and the line '(dont 4 d'ordre 4)' was redirected to the cover, where all vertices have order 4.

The sketches illustrate these decompositions:
- a 4-holed sphere with a seam;
- two spheres/pants glued along a disc with marked vertices;
- a handle/torus shape obtained from it.

Purpose: testing how hexagonal (pants) and square decompositions behave under branched double covers. This links the pants/hexagon picture of Teichmüller space with the maps/dessins and reflection-group picture of the previous page.

The word 'Justine' is written in mirror script at bottom left. It is presumably a name, possibly Justine Bumby, and is not mathematical.
errors: No mathematical errors: all vertex/edge/face counts satisfy Euler and Riemann–Hurwitz (−2 → −8 with 4 branch points; 2 → 0 with 4 branch points).
The initial 'triangles' in the bottom block was wrong (the faces must be quadrilaterals for the counts to work) and was corrected by Grothendieck himself to 'carrés'.

ideas.what: Decomposition of a pair of pants into two hexagons (6 vertices, 9 edges), and of a 4-holed sphere into 4 hexagons
ideas.modern_name: Right-angled hexagon decomposition of pants (Fenchel–Nielsen picture)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Fricke–Klein, Fenchel–Nielsen; standard in Teichmüller theory
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984) discusses pants decompositions and the Teichmüller tower at the level of ideas, not this computation

ideas.what: Lifting a cell decomposition along a double cover branched at 4 vertices, with Euler characteristic count
ideas.modern_name: Riemann–Hurwitz for branched covers of maps

ideas.what: Torus with regular 4-valent square map as double cover of the sphere (4 squares) branched at the 4 degree-2 vertices
ideas.modern_name: Pillowcase / elliptic curve as double cover of P^1 branched at 4 points; regular {4,4} map on the torus

deep.surprise_reason: Routine Euler-characteristic checks of standard constructions: hexagon decompositions of pants and the torus as a branched double cover of a square-decomposed sphere. Of mild interest only as a record of Grothendieck testing how pants/hexagon decompositions interact with maps and branched covers in 1983.
transcription_corrections: In the bottom-right block, 'dont 4 d'ordre 4' is struck through; '8 sommets d'ordre 4' refers to the cover, where all 8 vertices have order 4.
The top-left block reads '(dont 4 ramifiés) d'ordre' — the 'd'ordre' appears to be an unfinished/displaced phrase, probably 'd'ordre 2'.
'Justine' at bottom left is written in mirror script (non-mathematical).
